How to read this

Every camp below carries three numbers from the Forest Service list: how many people it holds when the Middle Fork Lodge gauge reads 2.5 ft or less, about 4 ft, and 6 ft or more. The feet are that gauge’s height (USGS 13309220), the number boaters trade, and the second number in a LateBoof reply (“2,800 cfs / 4.21 ft”). 21 of the 98 camps are gone at 6 ft or more, and 13 more shrink.

A blank on the list means the Forest Service gives no number: 33 camps have none at about 4 ft, and Indian Creek Beach has none at any level. Those show as “Not listed”, and the level filter leaves them out at that level rather than guess. Read the numbers either side.

The capacities are limits. A group may not use a camp rated for fewer people than it has. Groups top out at 24 on the Middle Fork, so a camp rated for 30 takes any permitted group. Each camp also carries the Forest Service’s use level for June and for July and August: low, mid, high or very high.

Requesting camps

Every camp on the Middle Fork is assigned; none is first-come. The River Office emails the permit holder a camp request form 14 days before the launch date, and builds your itinerary from it.

  • Complete the reservation on Recreation.gov and submit the camp request form at least 7 days before launch. The form can be submitted once. If it is late, or your requests do not fit your group or the rules, the River Clerk assigns the best camps left.
  • One hot-springs camp per group at most, and it is not guaranteed. Ask for three and you still get one at most.
  • During the lottery control season (May 28 to September 3) a group gets one night below Big Creek. The Forest Service web page puts that line at Big Creek, mile 77.9; its camp list draws it just below Last Chance, mile 78.
  • Layovers only at camps marked for them, case by case, and sparingly in the control season.
  • Groups of 12 or fewer are often put in smaller camps.
  • Heritage camps come with extra instructions to protect cultural sites. At the ten camps asterisked on the list, do not gather downed wood for fires.
  • An assigned camp is not exclusive. Backpackers and stock parties may share it, especially at hot springs and airstrips.
  • Camp assignments are final once the permit is issued, by email 5 or 6 days before launch.

Trip length follows group size: up to 8 days for 1–10 people, 7 days for 11–20, and 6 days for 21–24. Rules change; the Salmon-Challis National Forest page is the authority, and this summary was checked against it on 2026-09-30.

Picking camps for your group

Groups of 21 to 24
You need a camp rated for 30: 59 at 2.5 ft or less, 49 at about 4 ft, 50 at 6 ft or more. 48 hold 30 at every level.
Layover days
49 camps allow a layover, none of them in the Impassable Canyon. The ones that hold 30 at every level: Elkhorn Bar 8.2, Lake Creek 14.9, Johns Camp 15.2, Greyhound 15.9, Rapid River 16.5, Dolly Lake 19, Big Snag 19.1, Pistol Creek Camp 21.4, Airplane 23.9, Indian Creek Camp 26.2, Pungo Creek 27.4, Little Soldier 30.8, Marble Cr. Hot springs
One per trip: Trail Flat 6.9, Scout Camp 12.7, Sheepeater 13, Sunflower 32.6, Big Loon 49.3, Hospital Bar 52.1. These are close to a hot spring without being one of the six, so they do not use up your one: Lost Oak 32.6, Cow Creek 49.9, Cave Camp 51.8.

One night only below Big Creek. The aerials, and the photos still missing

Every camp has an aerial from the USDA’s National Agriculture Imagery Program, which is public domain. These were flown between 29 Sep 2021 and 2 Oct 2021, with the Middle Fork Lodge gauge at 1.4 ft (411–421 cfs), in the 2.5-ft-or-less column: they show the camps at low water. Each frame is 1.2 km across with north at the top. The Forest Service publishes river miles, not coordinates, so a frame is centred on the camp’s mile along the river’s mapped centerline, which is good to about a quarter mile: the camp is in the picture, near the middle, on the bank the entry names.

What an aerial cannot show is the camp from the boat, or the same beach at high water. Nobody publishes ground photos of these camps that can be reused, so each entry has room for a low-water and a high-water photograph, and they are empty.

Send one in. If you have a photo of a named camp, email it to owen@lateboof.com with the camp name, the date, and the flow if you know it. The same camp at two different levels is the most useful thing you can send. Corrections to anything on this page go to the same address.

Sources and what this is not

Mile, river side, all three capacities, layovers, the hot-springs, heritage and no-wood flags, and the use levels on every camp come from the Forest Service, Middle Fork Salmon Campsites (2025). It matches the table on the Forest Service’s Middle Fork page except that the web table leaves out Airplane camp. That the feet are the Middle Fork Lodge gauge’s height comes from GoRafting, Middle Fork of the Salmon River Flows & Levels and North Idaho Rivers. Camp names are spelled as that list spells them, because that is what the request form uses. The descriptions are LateBoof’s own wording; details beyond the Forest Service list were checked against GoRafting, Middle Fork of the Salmon River Rafting Guide, and where the two disagree the Forest Service figure is used and the camp says so.

Nothing here comes from a LateBoof trip yet. Beaches move, creeks blow out, and camps burn; a description is a starting point for a conversation with someone who was there last season, not a promise. Checked 2026-09-30.
